FROM MY DESK   Feigning stomach cramps on a frozen morning in eastern Ukraine, a young Russian lieutenant stepped away from his fellow soldiers into a line of bare trees—and waited. 

   Seconds later, a barrage of Ukrainian missiles obliterated the field behind him, leaving 68 dead and 60 wounded. His handler texted asking for an update. “There’s just meat,” he replied.

   Lt. Lev Stupnikov would go on to help Ukraine kill more than 300 Russian soldiers, making the 26-year-old one of the deadliest saboteurs in recent military history.

   Read Matthew Luxmoore’s incredible reporting for a rare window into Kyiv’s shadow war and Stupnikov’s daring escape across the front line into Ukrainian-held territory.

   • Fuel prices are up all over the U.S., but the surge is hitting some regions harder than others . And that impact could affect next month’s midterm elections.

   • Progress toward a U.S.-Mexico tariff deal has stalled after opposition from Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

   • Cornell University’s bid to rein in fraternities following gang-rape allegations is the latest in a long history of attempts to tame Greek life at the Ivy League school that have come up short.

   • Porsche’s new chief executive, Michael Leiters, is betting on luxury pricing and a tougher culture to revive the battered automaker .

READ IT HERE FIRST   The great Louvre robbery was just the start.   In the year since thieves stunned the world by smashing their way into the Louvre Museum and stealing France’s crown jewels worth at least $101 million, art heists have only intensified . From Wales to Sicily, more than 14 museums have been hit by smash-and-grab criminals since early 2025, suggesting museums haven’t cracked the code on how to safely protect their treasures. Police are still looking for the Louvre’s stolen trove of 19th-century jewelry, though French authorities arrested eight people in connection with the crime last October. But the subsequent art-crime onslaught across Europe suggests the Louvre heist wasn’t a one-off and might have emboldened copycats, as well as organized criminal gangs to target museums, reports Kelly Crow.

       5. MIDTERMS WATCH   Washington coverage chief Damian Paletta: The battle for the Senate is going to be an absolute nail-biter . There are growing indications, including from some Republicans, that the House will likely flip to Democratic control after the Nov. 3 midterms. Control of the Senate appears much less certain, though. Democrats feel confident they can pick up the seat in North Carolina, but there are so many other seats in play, including Michigan, where Republicans might be able to pull a blue seat over into their corner. President Trump is barnstorming the country, hopscotching through Montana, Nebraska and a number of other states. Former President Obama is slated to campaign in Michigan in the coming days for Abdul El-Sayed. A lot of these races are close, razor thin. Watch the candidates, not the polls. Are they acting desperate? Confident? That could tell you how comfortable they are in this final stretch. Democrats need to flip a net of four seats to control the Senate. That’s a real tall order.

Feigning stomach cramps on a frozen morning in eastern Ukraine, a young Russian lieutenant stepped away from his fellow soldiers into a line of bare trees—and waited.

6. SEE THE STORY

 

This tiny robot could fix massive sewer failures.

 
 
 

In January, a collapsed sewer pipe outside Washington, D.C., spilled more than 240 million gallons of raw sewage into the Potomac River. It is likely the largest sewage spill in U.S. history, but just one of an estimated 75,000 across the country each year, according to the EPA. Here’s how to get all the tax benefits from your health savings account.

 

Health savings accounts continue to gain ground with Americans—and with good reason, thanks to their triple tax benefits. While the accounts aren’t new, now is an opportune time to revisit their rules and wrinkles. Open enrollment is approaching for many employees, and favorable changes have taken effect for many self-employed workers and early retirees. Plus, even HSA owners who spend their funds each year can save on taxes. Whether you already have an account or are considering signing up for one, Laura Saunders outlines the key details.
